paper_title: miniTE: Diagnosing and Bridging the Execution Gap in Native NVFP4 Reinforcement Learning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Native NVFP4 promises to accelerate reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models (LLMs), but achieving stable learning across separate training and sampling engines remains challenging. We show that matching model weights and numerical formats is insufficient to ensure consistent policy evaluation, highlighting the importance of cross-engine numerical execution. We introduce miniTE, a lightweight framework that combines execution diagnostics, cross-engine numerical alignment, and efficient native W4A4 (4-bit weights and activations) GEMM computation for LLM RL. It improves numerical execution consistency without modifying the RL objective, while reducing implementation overhead to realize the benefits of native low-bit computation. Long-horizon RL experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate stable training and benchmark performance close to BF16, outperforming naive Transformer Engine (TE) NVFP4 in evaluation quality. On single NVIDIA B300 GPU node, the optimized learner reaches 33,540 tokens/s, yielding 1.39x and 1.47x the throughput of BF16 and TE NVFP4, respectively, for complete learner updates. We released the framework, kernels, diagnostics, and training configurations to make native low-bit RL easier.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Reinforcement learning is central to large language model (LLM) post-training, supporting instruction following (Ouyang et al., 2022) and mathematical reasoning (Shao et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2025). Repeated generation, policy evaluation, and updates (Yu et al., 2026) span an autoregressive sampler and learner that optimizes on sampled sequences. Native low-precision computation must accelerate these engines while preserving effective learning. Four-bit weight storage (Dettmers et al., 2023) and native four-bit training (Castro et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025) address different execution paths. Quantized sampling, matched precision, and quantization-aware RL address learnersampler mismatch (Huang et al., 2025; Xi et al., 2026; Zhuge et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2026); recent systems also support per-token NVFP4 and high-precision backward (Cursor Research, 2026; Li et al., 2026). We focus on native weight-and-activation four-bit (W4A4) expert computation, connecting cross-engine diagnosis, practical numerical path, and complete learner gains. RL makes cross-engine numerical behavior consequential. Probabilities computed by the learner and sampler enter importance ratios and clipping decisions (Schulman et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2025); implementation differences therefore enter optimization even at shared parameter version. Training inference mismatch and execution-aligned references have been studied in RL pipelines (Yao et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2026). NVFP4 adds choices in scale domains, rounding, accumulation, and operator composition that format name does not specify. This raises concrete question: which numerical dependencies must be exposed and controlled when native low-bit computation spans two execution engines? Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models combine continuous expert computation with discrete routing. Selective router precision and routing replay address sensitivity in expert selection (Fedus et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2025). We examine what remains after controlling parameter updates and matching assignments at the observed layer. Frozen-policy scoring shows that NVFP4 enlarges the cross-engine log-probability tail. Target-layer routing agreement leaves FC1/FC2 output discrepancies, and sampler-only scaling change does not establish agreement (Figure 1). These controls identify an execution specification, extending beyond bit width and expert IDs, as useful unit of diagnosis and implementation. Motivated by these findings, we introduce miniTE to connect this diagnosis with practical native NVFP4 training (Figure 2). Our framework checks quantized operands, expert outputs, and policy evaluation across the sampler and learner. Strict execution provides cross-engine reference for diagnosis; the default path combines our per-token quantization and native grouped-GEMM implementation with BF16 backward. Its purpose is stable, high-throughput learning under the existing RL objective. Arithmetic throughput is only one component of this cost: routed expert workloads also require operand preparation, representation conversion, and dispatch. We therefore optimize quantization and grouped GEMM as connected dataflow, reducing repeated preparation around the numerical core so that FP4 arithmetic gains translate into faster learner updates. Comparisons between our initial and optimized operator implementations check the numerical effects of those changes. Long-horizon Qwen3-30B-A3B runs show sustained learning with miniTE and higher mathematical evaluation scores than naive NVFP4. Same-recipe module comparisons show 2.46 expert-forward speedup over TE U3045. Complete learner updates on fixed text reach 1.39 BF16 throughput in the optimized configuration and 1.33 in repeated core study. The module comparison measures native implementation gains; complete learner updates measure the numerical path and implementation together. Separate colocated RL measurements identify weight conversion and synchronization as an integration bottleneck. Our contributions are: 1. Execution-gap diagnosis. Frozen-policy, routing-conditioned, and scaling controls identify numerical differences beyond nominal NVFP4 recipe agreement; strict execution supplies an actionable alignment reference. 2. Practical native NVFP4 RL. An integrated W4A4 expert-forward path with BF16 backward sustains long-horizon learning and improves all four mathematics benchmarks over naive NVFP4 without modifying the RL objective. 3. lightweight framework with numerically faithful acceleration. miniTE exposes configurable numerical recipes, replaceable expert operators, and reusable diagnostics for developing custom low-bit training settings. Operator-level numerical checks and complete learner benchmarks substantiate its execution optimizations. We release Dockerfiles, reference configurations, and single-command launch scripts to support reproducible experiments and extensions across the supported low-bit RL paths.

sections.title: 3 Diagnosing the Execution Gap
sections.content: The frozen-policy study scores identical token sequences under teacher forcing with frozen Qwen3-30BA3B-Base checkpoint (Yang et al., 2025). Tails use 32 prompts and 69,088 matched tokens; localization uses 12 prompts at 11 depths. Confidence intervals use 2,000 prompt-cluster bootstrap resamples. Within-stack self-comparisons are bitwise exact. Appendix specifies the collectors and full protocol.

The paired increase is 0.1641, with 95% confidence interval of [0.1311, 0.2005]. NVFP4 therefore amplifies the log-probability tail beyond the BF16 cross-engine floor before any optimizer update takes place. 𝑡 Figure 1 Execution differences survive recipe and routing agreement. sections.title: 3.2 Are Recipe and Routing Agreement Sufficient?
sections.content: Matched routing leaves operator differences. We fix expert assignments at each target layer while retaining its naturally accumulated inputs. FC1 symmetric relative-𝐿2 discrepancies range from 0.0381 to 0.6124, and FC2 discrepancies from 0.0810 to 0.7624 (Figure 1, right). Matched assignments therefore leave residual output differences. Natural routing additionally shows changing expert selections and nonmonotonic depthdependent divergence. separate replay at common MoE-layer input also leaves FC1/FC2 differences between learner modules and the sampler reference (Appendix C). Finer scales alone do not establish consistency. Changing only the sampler activation outer scale from per-tensor to per-token leaves FC1/FC2 discrepancies unchanged; the tail change is inconclusive on this fourprompt cohort. The early per-token candidate also retains larger tail than standard NVFP4 (Appendix C). 3 These controls motivate specifying the complete operator path: finer scales alone do not establish cross-engine agreement. Implication for the training path. These findings motivate specifying the operands and composition that define each execution. miniTE makes these choices explicit and implements native training path, evaluated for learning behavior and cost in Section 5.

sections.title: 4 MINITE: A Practical Native NVFP4 RL Framework
sections.content: Section 3 motivates making the executed numerical path explicit. We choose native recipe whose activation scales depend on each token row, and jointly optimize the cost of executing it. Figure 2 connects this numerical specification to diagnostic interfaces and the native expert-computation dataflow.

sections.title: 4.1 Execution Specification and Diagnostic References
sections.content: Operands and composition. An execution specification records scale domains, rounding, logical layouts, and the placement of casts and router coefficients. Comparisons fix the weight version, token IDs, and scoring context, then decode codes and scales to common layout. Input provenance and expert IDs identify the comparison boundary: naturally accumulated inputs reveal cross-engine differences, while common-input comparisons test the operators applied at that boundary. This distinction follows directly from the residual differences under matched target-layer routing. Two complementary references. The strict execution reference matches learner kernels, formulas, and reduction orders to the sampler, including surrounding normalization and communication paths. It retains native NVFP4 expert forward and BF16 gradients, and provides cross-engine intervention evaluated in Section 5.4. The operator reference instead compares initial and optimized implementations on common inputs under fixed recipe. It tests whether an API or layout transformation preserves quantized operands and outputs. The practical learner below is evaluated as complete learning configuration; its implementation checks use the latter reference.

sections.title: 4.3 Joint Design of Quantization and Grouped GEMM
sections.content: Routed expert computation requires operand preparation and scheduling in addition to matrix multiplication. Expert-dependent group sizes, empty groups, and padding affect the interface between these operations. We optimize that interface as connected dataflow. shared producerconsumer representation. The reference quantizer already processes grouped inputs, but returns expert views or lists from which grouped GEMM reconstructs its arguments. miniTE writes packed FP4 codes, block scales, and outer-scale information directly into contiguous buffers consumed by GEMM. Device-side offsets describe expert boundaries, and metadata storage and workspaces are reused. This removes repeated splitting and argument preparation between two grouped interfaces while retaining expert-dependent offsets and padding, including support for empty groups. Statistics travel with their activations. The FC1 reference permutes tokens, pads them, and scans the padded rows for maxima. miniTE collects maxima during permutation and pads both the activations and statistics:

sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate learning behavior, complete learner efficiency, and the numerical and performance effects of the implementation design. The frozen comparisons in Section 3 establish the problem; the experiments here evaluate the training configurations and execution paths.

sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: Native low-precision learning. Microscaling specifies narrow elements and shared block scales (Rouhani et al., 2023). QLoRA uses four-bit storage with BF16 computation (Dettmers et al., 2023), whereas Quartet executes native MXFP4 forward and gradient GEMMs (Castro et al., 2025). NVFP4 pretraining (NVIDIA et al., 2025), Composer 2 (Cursor Research, 2026), and Miles (Li et al., 2026) provide native low-bit learning paths. Miles combines per-token NVFP4, high-precision backward, and quantizer agreement. miniTE studies residual cross-engine execution differences and the implementation cost of the native expert path. Quantized RL. QeRL combines quantized rollout with low-rank adaptation (Huang et al., 2025); Jet-RL unifies FP8 training and rollout (Xi et al., 2026). QUADS combines learner-side W4A16 weight QAT with sampler-side activation residual compensation (Zhuge et al., 2026). QaRL pairs low-bit forward computation with sequence-level trust-band optimization (Gu et al., 2026). miniTE evaluates native W4A4 expert-forward computation with BF16 backward and retains the existing TIS-corrected RL pipeline. Execution mismatch and routing. Off-policy analysis (Yao et al., 2025), sequence-level ratios (Zheng et al., 2025), and execution-aligned references (Zhong et al., 2026) examine samplerlearner consistency. FP16 studies address rounding precision (Qi et al., 2025); selective precision (Fedus et al., 2022) and routing replay (Ma et al., 2025) address expert selection. Deterministic kernels control dependence on execution context (He & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025; SGLang Team, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). Our diagnosis identifies residual differences under matched target-layer assignments, while the native implementation is evaluated through operator equivalence, learning traces, and complete learner timing.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: Frozen-policy and routing-conditioned measurements expose execution differences beyond nominal NVFP4 agreement. We introduced miniTE, combining cross-engine diagnostics, native W4A4 forward with independently selected backward precision, and jointly optimized quantization and grouped GEMM. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, miniTE sustained learning over long RL training horizon and outperformed standard TE NVFP4 on all four mathematics benchmarks, with five-task average close to that of BF16. The optimized learner achieves 1.47 the throughput of TE NVFP4 and 1.39 that of BF16. Separate expert-forward measurements under the same recipe show 2.46 speedup over Transformer Engine. With configurable recipes, replaceable operators, and reproducible launch environments, miniTE provides an extensible foundation for numerical and systems co-design in native low-bit RL.

sections.title: 8 Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: Numerical fidelity beyond execution alignment. Although miniTE improves mathematical evaluation over standard TE NVFP4, its practical path still falls short of BF16 in average evaluation quality and of strict execution in cross-engine agreement. Matching execution does not eliminate the quantization error associated with E2M1 values and E4M3 block scales. However, the remaining quality gap does not isolate the effects of quantization error from residual execution differences. Future work should investigate tighter execution alignment together with format-aware error compensation, aiming to improve learning quality while retaining native W4A4 computation. End-to-end efficiency and hardware-aware fusion. Our colocated measurements identify weight conversion and synchronization as substantial integration cost. These measurements cover selected stages rather than complete RL iterations, so component speedups alone do not establish end-to-end gains. Reducing repeated conversion and packing at learnersampler boundaries is therefore priority. Online amaxquantization GEMM fusion offers complementary direction for reducing operator-side preparation costs. Its numerical behavior and performance need joint validation, particularly when scales evolve during accumulation. Efficient implementations must coordinate scale updates, accumulator rescaling, and data movement within SM resource constraints, motivating further hardwaresoftware co-design. Our learning evidence covers one MoE model with one run per configuration, and the implementation gains are evaluated on Blackwell hardware. Broader validation across models, tasks, independent training seeds, and hardware platforms remains future work.

The strict execution configuration runs without TIS.
